hints: Start by looking at the top plateau of each curve in Fig. 3.1 - which two curves eventually reach the same maximum rate if you add enough substrate, and which one stays much lower no matter how much substrate is added?
walkthrough:
Recall What Each Inhibitor Does to the Curve**
Think of the active site as a lock. A competitive inhibitor fits into the lock itself, so adding lots more substrate keys can push it out. That means at very high substrate concentration the rate can still reach the normal maximum. A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and twists the lock, so even with lots of substrate fewer working enzymes are available and the maximum stays low.

Match X, Y and Z**
Curve X is fastest at low substrate and plateaus at 10 au - that is the normal uninhibited enzyme. Curve Y is slower at first but eventually catches up to the same 10 au plateau at high substrate - that is competitive inhibition overcome by substrate. Curve Z plateaus at only about 5 au and never catches up - that is non-competitive inhibition.
Final answer: non-competitive inhibitor: Z; competitive inhibitor: Y; without any inhibitor: X.

hints: First read the plateau value for each curve on the y-axis - that is $V_{max}$. Which curves share the same plateau?
Next remember how to find $K_m$ from the graph - it is the substrate concentration on the x-axis that gives half of $V_{max}$. Try halving each $V_{max}$ and reading across then down.
Compare the numbers you read off - look for which pair shares the same $V_{max}$ and which pair shares the same $K_m$, quoting values with units.
Link $K_m$ to biology - a higher $K_m$ means more substrate is needed to reach half $V_{max}$, so what does that tell you about affinity for substrate?
walkthrough:
Compare $V_{max}$ - Read the Plateaus**
$V_{max}$ is the flat top of the curve where all active sites are saturated. From Fig. 3.1, X levels off at 10 arbitrary units and Y also levels off at 10 au at high substrate concentration around 20-25 $\text{mmol dm}^{-3}$. Z levels off at only 5 au. So X and Y share the same $V_{max}$, which is double that of Z.

Compare $K_m$ - Find Half $V_{max}$**
$K_m$ is the substrate concentration needed for half $V_{max}$. For X, half $V_{max}$ = 5 au, which occurs at about 4 $\text{mmol dm}^{-3}$. For Z, half $V_{max}$ = 2.5 au, which also occurs at about 4 $\text{mmol dm}^{-3}$. So X and Z have the same $K_m$. For Y, half $V_{max}$ = 5 au, which occurs at a higher concentration of about 6.5 $\text{mmol dm}^{-3}$. So Y has a higher $K_m$ than X and Z.

Link to Affinity**
A low $K_m$ means only a little substrate is needed to get to half speed, so the enzyme has high affinity for substrate. Because Y has the highest $K_m$, it has the lowest affinity. This fits competitive inhibition - inhibitor and substrate compete for the active site, so apparent affinity falls.

Final answer: $V_{max}$: X and Y have same $V_{max}$ of 10 au, which is higher than Z at 5 au. $K_m$: X and Z have same $K_m$ of 4 $\text{mmol dm}^{-3}$, which is lower than Y, indicating higher affinity for substrate in X/Z than Y.

hints: Start from the smallest building block - what monomer makes up DNA and what three parts does each monomer contain?
Think about how those monomers are joined into a long strand, and then how two strands are held together in the middle.
Recall the famous 3D shape and the way the two strands run relative to each other.
Remember the pairing rule in the centre - which base always pairs with which, and what type of bond holds each pair?
walkthrough:
Start With Nucleotides**
DNA is a polynucleotide, meaning a long chain of nucleotide monomers. Each DNA nucleotide has three parts: the pentose sugar deoxyribose, a phosphate group, and a nitrogen-containing base - adenine, thymine, cytosine or guanine.

Build the Backbone and Helix**
Nucleotides join by phosphodiester bonds between the sugar of one and the phosphate of the next, forming a sugar-phosphate backbone. Two such strands twist together to form a double helix, and they run antiparallel - one runs 3' to 5' while the other runs 5' to 3'.

Hold the Centre Together**
The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between the bases pointing inward. Bases pair in a fixed complementary way: adenine always pairs with thymine and cytosine always pairs with guanine. A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, keeping the helix width constant.

Final answer: DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel polynucleotide strands. Each strand has a sugar-phosphate backbone joined by phosphodiester bonds. Strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases: A-T and C-G. Nucleotides consist of deoxyribose, phosphate and a nitrogenous base.

hints: Think about what hydrogen peroxide does to the DNA molecule itself and what can go wrong when the cell tries to fix that break.
Connect a permanent change in nucleotide sequence to the genetic definition of a mutation - a new allele and possibly an altered protein.
walkthrough:
From Damage to Permanent Change**
Hydrogen peroxide is reactive and can break the DNA strands or damage bases. When repair enzymes try to fix this, they can make a mistake and put in the wrong nucleotide. If not corrected before replication, that becomes a permanent change in the base sequence of DNA.

Why That Means Mutagen**
A mutagen is defined as any agent that increases the rate of mutation, and a gene mutation is a change in nucleotide sequence that creates a new allele. Because the altered DNA sequence can be transcribed and translated into an altered amino acid sequence and polypeptide, hydrogen peroxide fits the definition of a mutagen.

Final answer: Hydrogen peroxide damages/breaks DNA and errors in repair insert an incorrect nucleotide / change the base sequence, forming a new allele, which may give an altered polypeptide. Hence it causes mutation so is a mutagen.
